bib.title: The Price Reversal Phenomenon: When Cheaper Reasoning Models Cost More

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "The Price Reversal Phenomenon: When Cheaper Reasoning Models End Up Costing More", Lingjiao Chen (Stanford, Microsoft Research), Chi Zhang (CMU), Yeye He (Microsoft Research), Ion Stoica and Matei Zaharia (UC Berkeley), James Zou (Stanford). arXiv:2603.23971v2 [cs.CL], 28 May 2026. Preprint, no venue stated. File: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/08-eval/sources/chen-2026-price-reversal-phenomenon.pdf

COVERAGE: 69,131 of 69,131 chars read, all 22 pages, including both appendices, limitations and the reference list. The reference list was skimmed. Text extraction was clean. Figure panels extracted as loose numbers, but the captions were read.

TARGET NOTE (generative-ai/08-eval/notes/09-reading-results.md)
- Sections: error bar on a pass rate; how many tasks; paired differences; repeats and clustering; slice before you conclude; read the transcripts; benchmark report to hypotheses; report template; checklist; pitfalls.
- Already covers: sampling error, paired tests, repeats, slices, and "weigh each fix's gain against its cost". The report template has a "Cost per success" row. The "Compare on the same tasks" section pairs on accuracy only.
- Lacks: any treatment of cost as a measured, noisy quantity. Cost is treated as a single number, never as a distribution.
- Best-fit section: "From a benchmark report to hypotheses", step 4 (weigh each fix's gain against its cost) and the model-swap paragraph. A second fit is "Repeats and clustering", as a cost counterpart to the "repeats reduce noise" point.
- Better-fit note: 06-evaluating-agents.md. It already has a Cost per success metric row, the Kapoor et al. "AI Agents That Matter" and Holistic Agent Leaderboard paragraphs ("Plot accuracy against cost"), and a worked cost-per-success exercise. This paper extends that paragraph directly (listed price is not cost; cost per query is stochastic). 10-evals-in-ci.md (efficiency budget "cost per success ≤ 1.2 × baseline") is a secondary fit. The sharpest use is a short paragraph in 06 and a one-line cross-reference in 09. Per the repo rule, the citation and a references row are needed wherever it lands.

CORE CLAIM: Listed per-token price (input + output) is an unreliable proxy for what a workload actually costs. Reasoning models differ widely in thinking tokens and in agent turns, so a cheaper-listed model often costs more. Per-query cost is also a random variable, so predicting it means predicting a distribution.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. Price reversal is common.
 - number: 106 of 336 pairwise comparisons (32%) reversed.
 - setup: 8 models (GPT-5.4, GPT-5.4 Mini, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Gemini 3 Flash, Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Haiku 4.5, Kimi K2.6, MiniMax M2.7), 12 tasks (9 single-turn, 3 agentic), cost only (accuracy ignored), prices as of 2026-05-01. "Listed price" is input price plus output price per MTok.
 - quote: "Of these, 106 comparisons (32%) exhibit pricing reversal, i.e., the model with lower listed price actually incurs a higher total cost."
 - where: p4.
2. Headline example.
 - number: Gemini 3 Flash is listed at $3.50 against GPT-5.4 at $17.50, but its actual cost is $705 against $509 (+38%).
 - setup: total over all 12 tasks.
 - quote: "Gemini 3 Flash's list price ($3.5/1 million tokens) is 80% cheaper than GPT-5.4 ($17.5), but its actual cost ($705) is actually 38% higher than GPT-5.4 ($509)."
 - where: Fig 1 caption, p2.
3. The reversal rate varies by task, and the cost ranking is task-dependent.
 - number: 11% (ArenaHard) to 57% (MMLU-Pro).
 - quote: "The reversal rate varies across tasks, ranging from 11% on ArenaHard to 57% on MMLUPro."
 - where: p5.
 - supporting: "Gemini 3 Flash is the second cheapest model according to the API listed pricing, but it is the most expensive one on MMLUPro." Gemini 3 Flash costs $219 on MMLU-Pro against $44 for GPT-5.4. On Cybench, Kimi K2.6 is listed 72% cheaper than GPT-5.4 but costs "2x more".
4. Cause: thinking tokens dominate single-turn tasks, and turns plus cached context dominate agentic tasks.
 - number: more than 95% of the gap on reversed single-turn pairs is thinking tokens. Turns account for more than 80% of the Kimi K2.6 vs GPT-5.4 gap on Cybench.
 - method: Shapley-value attribution over 8 cost factors (turns, fresh input, output, cached tokens, thinking tokens, three prices). Cost is multilinear in the factors, so there is a closed form.
 - quote: "More than 95% of the cost difference among reversed model pairs is attributed to thinking tokens."
 - where: Fig 3 caption p7.
 - example: "it takes Gemini 3 Flash more than 60,000 thinking tokens to solve an specific MMLU Pro problem, while GPT 5.4 needs only 25 tokens" (p2). This is one query, not an average. Table 5 gives totals: MMLU-Pro thinking tokens are 71,489k for Gemini 3 Flash against 1,804k for GPT-5.4.
5. The same query run repeatedly on the same model gives widely varying cost.
 - number: up to 9.7x between the cheapest and most expensive run.
 - setup: repeated rollouts of a fixed (model, query) pair, shown on AIME and Terminal-Bench 2.0 for three models; within-query CV "routinely above 0.3".
 - quote: "The cost spans up to 9.7x between the cheapest and most expensive run, with within-query coefficient of variation routinely above 0.3."
 - where: §5.1, p7-8.
 - consequence: "individual reversal verdicts can flip across runs". The number of repeats is not stated in the text.
6. The mean hides the reversal at the quantiles a per-query budget cares about.
 - number: pooled reversal is 31.5% on the mean and about 39-40% at Q15-Q40 (peak 39.6% at Q40). It is lowest at Q99, 25.0%.
 - quote: "On the body of the cost distribution (Q15-Q40, the quantiles a per-query budget actually hits), reversal jumps from 31.5% to 39-40%."
 - where: §5.2 p8, Fig 9 and Table 6, appendix.
7. Multi-turn mechanism (appendix E; asserted, with diagnostic figures only in the code repo).
 - quote: "The reversal magnitude is also worse on incorrect runs (3-10x cost gaps for incorrect reversed pairs vs. within 2x for correct ones)."
 - where: p18-19.
 - related: cheaper-listed models hit the message cap more often, and replayed history is the largest cost component. Per-task cost "grows faster than linearly with the turn count".
8. Task difficulty.
 - claim: hard tasks amplify the turn contribution; easy tasks show much less reversal.
 - setup: easy means 6-8 of the 8 models answer correctly, medium 3-5, hard 0-2.
 - quote: "On the easy questions, the price reversal becomes much less."
 - where: p7.
9. Scale of the study: more than 7.39B tokens, 6,877 unique tasks, over $5,000 spend, 190,000 turn-level API calls, run Feb-May 2026 (p15). Code and data are "will release", not yet verified as released.

LIMITS
- Stated (appendix G):
 - "Pricing is a single snapshot (May 1, 2026)".
 - "Each model is run at a single reasoning setting" (OpenAI at reasoning_effort high; the rest at defaults or adaptive thinking), so the effort-versus-cost trade-off is not studied.
 - "Cost is decoupled from quality". The authors argue that adding quality would only strengthen their finding, but they do not test it.
- Unstated:
 - Cost only. There is no cost-per-correct-answer analysis, even though accuracy was graded. Cost-of-pass (Erol et al.) is cited but not computed.
 - One run per task as the base case, and the base-case verdict is therefore noisy by the paper's own §5.1. No confidence intervals on the 32%.
 - Shapley attribution explains a mean gap, not tail risk (§5.3 admits quantile attribution is unavailable).
 - Agentic scaffolds are fixed. Opus 4.7 has a 32,000 thinking-token cap, Kimi and MiniMax 128,000, and Terminus 2 has no explicit turn limit while ReAct uses a 1,000-message limit. Differences in caps affect cost.
 - Caching is not exercised in single-turn tasks.
 - Models and pricing will date quickly. The mechanism (thinking tokens, turns) is the durable part.
 - Subsets are used for MMLU-Pro (3,000), HLE (500) and SimpleQA (500), and for AIME just 60 tasks. Agentic suites are small (Cybench 39, Terminal-Bench 89, GAIA 165), so per-task rankings there are noisy.
 - Grading: HLE, SimpleQA and ArenaHard use a Gemini 3.1 Pro judge at low effort. The judge is also one of the evaluated models.

BUILDS ON: Shapley (1953) for the attribution. Data Shapley (Ghorbani and Zou 2019), SHAP (Lundberg and Lee 2017) for use in ML. FrugalML (Chen et al. 2020), FrugalGPT (Chen et al. 2024b) and the routing literature, which assumes known per-query cost. Cost-of-pass (Erol et al. 2026). Overthinking (Chen et al. 2024c, "Do not think that much for 2+3=?"; Sui et al. 2025). Test-time scaling (Muennighoff et al. 2025, s1). Compound AI systems (Zaharia et al. 2024). Benchmarks: AIME, ARC-AGI, GPQA, ArenaHard, HLE, LiveCodeBench, LiveMathBench, MMLU-Pro, SimpleQA, GAIA, Cybench, Terminal-Bench 2.0. Note that it does not cite Kapoor et al. (AI Agents That Matter; HAL), the closest prior cost-accuracy work already in note 06.

CODE: none beyond the cost formula, which is worth keeping. The text printed "C(F)=T·[n_in·p_in + (n_out + n_think)·p_out + n_cache·p_cache]" (eq. 3, p5) and the agentic cost with cache write and read (eq. 2, p3-4).

FIGURES (captions via the figures script)
- Fig 1 (p2): listed-price rank against actual-cost rank across all 12 tasks. This is the best candidate. The crossing lines show the reversal in one glance. Totals: Opus $708, Gemini 3 Flash $705, Gemini 3.1 Pro $677, GPT-5.4 $509, Kimi $422, Haiku $421, GPT-5.4 Mini $325, MiniMax $148.
- Fig 2 (p4): reversal rate per task, plus MMLU-Pro and Cybench slope charts. The MMLU-Pro and Cybench panels show the ranking flips between tasks.
- Fig 5 (p8): per-query cost spread for a fixed model and query. This is the one for the "repeats" point in note 09.
- Fig 9 (p20): reversal rate by cost quantile, which shows the mean hides the body of the distribution.
- Fig 3 (p7) and Fig 4 (p8): Shapley breakdown by factor and by difficulty. Fig 7 is per-dataset.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions found.
- Internal inconsistencies:
 - §3 says "roughly one in five cost judgments ... would be wrong", but 32% is about one in three. Appendix G says "roughly one third".
 - The abstract says 32%, but 106/336 = 31.5%, and Fig 9 uses 31.5%.
 - 28 "model pairs" is described as both unordered (C(8,2)) and "28 ordered" in Fig 9; the 336 count comes from 28 pairs x 12 tasks.
 - The Fig 2 caption says "Gemini 3.1 Flash" where the models are Gemini 3 Flash or 3.1 Pro.
 - The Fig 1 caption lists "Human Last Exam" and only some of the tasks.
 - The intro says GPT-5.4's cost is "70%" of Gemini 3 Flash, while 509/705 = 72%.
- The abstract's "reversal magnitude reaching up to 28x" and "900% more thinking tokens" are not located or derived anywhere in the body text. The text only supports a 4x (Gemini 3 Flash vs Haiku 4.5 on MMLU-Pro) and a 5x example. Do not cite 28x without checking Fig 6 and the released data.
- "Over 10x on the same prompt" (intro) against "9.7x" (abstract, §5.1) differ slightly.
- Several numbers sit only in figure axis labels (extraction is clean but panel titles are shifted after their data in Fig 6). Table 5 and Table 6 are readable.
- Code and data are described as "will release", so unverified.
